analytic.title: Fine-scale population genetic structure in a wide-ranging carnivore, the leopard (Panthera pardus fusca) in central India

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Aim Habitat loss and fragmentation can influence the genetic structure of biological populations. Large terrestrial predators can often avoid genetic subdivision due to fragmentation because they have high rates of dispersal-mediated gene flow. Leopards (Panthera pardus) are found in a variety of habitats and are the most widely distributed of the large and middle-sized felids. We investigated the genetic diversity and population substructure of leopards (P.p fusca) in a fragmented meta-population comprised of four populations from five protected areas and inter-connecting corridors spread over an area of 45,000 km 2 in central India.
Location Kanha, Pench, Satpura and Melghat Tiger Reserves, and interconnecting corridors in the Satpura-Maikal Landscape of Central India.

Methods We collected faecal samples and used genetic methods to identify individuals, estimate the genetic variation and evaluate the patterns of genetic substructuring within this meta-population of leopards.

div.head: Results
div.p: We identified 217 individual leopards using a panel of seven microsatellite loci. Leopards showed high levels of genetic diversity in all sampled populations. Spatial and non-spatial Bayesian analysis revealed at least two admixed genetic populations with indications of ongoing genetic subdivision. Genetic differentiation between populations was not explained by geographic distance. We identified nine individuals as migrants, most of which were assigned to reserves connected by corridors.

Main conclusions Our study demonstrates that the leopard, an adaptable and vagile species, can become genetically differentiated with increased habitat fragmentation. Contrary to our hypothesis of panmixia, our results indicate that although leopards in this landscape are admixed, there is genetic substructuring at both the landscape and the fine-scale level. We conclude that this is due to habitat fragmentation and corridors are of immense value in maintaining genetic connectivity in this landscape.

div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: Many large carnivores currently exist within fragmented habitats much too small to support long-term persistence. Fragmented populations are at risk of local extinction due to demographic, genetic and stochastic environmental events.

Habitat fragmentation has been linked to the loss of genetic variation in several highly vagile species, including Ethiopian wolves Canis simenesis (Gottelli et al., 1994), pumas Puma concolor (Ernest et al., 2000), Eurasian lynx Lynx lynx (Spong & Hellborg, 2002), brown bears Ursus arctos (Miller & Waits, 2003) and jaguars Panthera onca (Haag et al., 2010).

The leopard (Panthera pardus) is a habitat generalist and has the widest geographical distribution of the Panthera cats. Its distribution historically extended through most of Sub-Saharan Africa, along parts of the North African coast, through Central, South and Southeast Asia, and north to the Amur River valley in Russia (Sunquist & Sunquist, 2002). While similar morphologically, the leopard differs in mass by a factor of about 1-4 in same-sex adult pairings from its larger sympatric congeners, the lion (Panthera leo) in Africa and India and the tiger (Panthera tigris) in Asia. The leopard has a wider fundamental niche than its larger congeners in terms of areas and habitats it occupies. Lions and tigers compete directly and indirectly with leopards wherever they coexist. Where leopards coexist with tigers and lions, they do so by feeding on smaller or different prey, shifting space and micro-habitat use, and adjusting their activity patterns to reduce encounters (Seidensticker, 1976;Bailey, 1993;Karanth & Sunquist, 2000). Both lions and tigers kill leopards, and the smaller leopard is socially subordinate to the larger congeners (Palomares & Caro, 1999). Subadult leopards exhibit exploratory movements that result in a proficient dispersal system that facilitates the location of suitable habitat patches not inhabited by the larger congeners or by other same-sex adult leopards (Bailey, 1993).

One consequence of social subordination is that the leopard appears to show greater plasticity or ability to change behaviour as conditions change (Seidensticker, 1976). In the Indian subcontinent, leopards (P.p. fusca) inhabit both intact and degraded forest habitats; where wild prey are scarce (Singh, 2005;Athreya et al., 2011), they switch from killing wild prey to killing similarly sized domestic stock, such as calves and goats (Seidensticker et al., 1990). One example is the leopards living in Sanjay Gandhi National Park, which abuts the Mumbai megalopolis, where they prey on domestic dogs and pigs (Edgaonkar & Chellam, 2002).

In Tanzania, leopards were reported to have high levels of heterozygosity, no genetic structuring, high numbers of migrants, and no evidence of genetic bottleneck or isolation between populations at a country-wide scale (Spong et al., 2000). This study suggested that leopards in Tanzania occur as a continuous population that exchanges genes throughout the country via high migration rates. Indian leopards are not as adversely affected by deteriorating and fragmenting habitat conditions as tigers are (Ramakrishnan et al., 1999), and are reported to have high genetic variation (Mondol et al., 2009;Dutta et al., 2012). We asked the question: Does the leopard's dispersal proficiency and its ability to inhabit degraded habitat and subsist on medium to small-sized wild and domestic prey manifest itself in genetic homogeneity over a regional landscape scale? We investigated the population structure of the leopard in four populations in five large protected areas, some of which are inter-connected by forested corridors in the central Indian landscape by analysing DNA obtained non-invasively through field-collected faecal samples.

The central Indian highlands are a major refugia for India's large mammal assemblage, and one of the country's major biotic provinces (Rodgers et al., 2002). Historically, this landscape was forested and occupied by tigers and leopards (Forsyth, 1871;Dunbar-Brander, 1923). Recently, Jhala et al. (2008) identified Kanha-Pench and Satpura-Melghat as important sublandscapes for tigers in this region. Jhala et al. (2011) suggested that leopard distribution is largely contiguous in this landscape with protected areas serving as population source sites. With increased human population and related development, the forests in this area have become highly fragmented over the past few centuries. However, because leopards are known to exist in degraded habitat, often in close proximity to human settlements, and based on previous genetic studies of leopards in Tanzania, we hypothesized high genetic variability and panmixia among leopards in this landscape.

A solitary lifestyle and cryptic behaviour have made previous research on leopards difficult, but recent advances in obtaining genetic data through non-invasive sources such as scats, shed hair, urine and even saliva (Morin et al., 1993;Bricker et al., 1996;Hayakawa & Takenaka, 1999;Sundqvist et al., 2008) have facilitated sampling species that are difficult and expensive to trap in order to collect tissue or blood samples. Advances in genetic analyses and statistical techniques, including population-assignment tests, have made it possible to identify the origin of animals by assigning them to a population based on their multilocus genotypes (Paetkau et al., 1995;Waser & Strobeck, 1998;Waser et al., 2001) and to identify cryptic population boundaries (Manel et al., 2003;Proctor et al., 2005). These new techniques enabled us to explore leopard population genetic structure in central India.

div.head: Study area
div.p: We conducted our study in a landscape of approximately 45,000 km 2 in the Satpura-Maikal landscape of Central India (21.15 N -76.50 E, 22.80 N -81.05 E). Narmada and Tapti are the major rivers in this landscape, the catchment of which is formed by the Satpura Range in the north and Maikal Range to the east (Krishnan, 1982). The Vindhyachal Range runs parallel and north of the Satpura Range, separated by the Narmada floodplain. Altitude varies from 320 to 1352 msl and topography ranges from plains, undulating plateaus and grasslands to precipitous cliffs. Temperature ranges from 2 °C in the winter to 48 °C in the summer, marked by an intervening monsoon season (June-August) when the area receives 1000-2200 mm of rainfall. Forest types vary from dry deciduous mixed forest, dry deciduous teak (Tectona grandis) forests, to moist peninsular sal (Shorea robusta) forest.

We sampled four leopard populations in five Tiger Reserves (TRs) in two central Indian states: Madhya Pradesh (MP) and Maharashtra (Mh) (Fig. 1). These TRs are Satpura (1428 km 2 , MP), Melghat (1677 km 2 , Mh), Pench (758 km 2 , MP; 258 km 2 , Mh) and Kanha (2059 km 2 , MP). Although Pench TR is physically present in two states (MP and Mh), the leopard population is contiguous between the two states, and we treated it as one unit in this study to make it biologically meaningful. Satpura and Melghat are located on the western edge and Kanha and Pench on the eastern edge of this landscape, and these two pairs of TRs are each inter-connected by a forest corridor (Fig. 1). Satpura is also connected by a corridor to Pench, while there is patchy connectivity between Melghat and Pench. Leopards and their prey species were reported from these corridors (Jhala et al., 2011). The matrix between the eastern and western pair of TRs has some tracts of forests but is highly populated and contains numerous small cities, towns and villages along with dams, mines and other industries. The soil is agriculturally very productive, and large areas of forest have been converted into cultivation.

div.head: Field methods
div.p: Because direct sighting and sampling from wild leopards are very difficult, we used non-invasive faecal sampling as a source for DNA. During April-June 2009 and Nov 2009-May 2010, we (the first and second author, with the assistance of forest staff) sampled along existing forest trails and roads on foot and by vehicles, collecting felid (leopard and tiger) scats from the TRs and the corridors. We used systematic sampling inside the TRs using a 10 km 2 grid as the sampling unit. We sampled all the grids inside the TRs at least once except those that were completely occupied by dense human populations, barren-land, inaccessible terrain or water bodies. We used stratified random sampling in corridors. Each corridor was stratified based on previous information about leopard occupancy (Jhala et al., 2008); grids with known occupancy were searched preferentially. Our sampling covered 15,000 km of trails and represented c. 8000 km 2 of the total area of 45,000 km 2 . In the field, we identified felid scats by their morphology and associated signs such as scrapes and pugmarks. The GPS location of each scat was recorded. Samples were stored in absolute ethanol until DNA extraction.

div.head: Genetic methods
div.p: We extracted genomic DNA using the QIAamp mini-stool kit (Qiagen Inc., Valencia, CA, USA) following the manufacturer's instructions. DNA samples were first screened for species identification using a leopard-specific FAM-labelled NADH4 marker (Mondol et al., 2009) that amplifies a 130 bp fragment and a tiger-specific TET-labelled NADH5 marker (Mukherjee et al., 2007) that amplifies a 160 bp fragment. Samples that were confirmed as leopards in duplicate runs along with a positive and negative control were then screened with a panel of seven microsatellite loci. Details of individual identification, error rates and characteristics of the microsatellites are described in Dutta et al. (2012) and available in Table S1.

All PCRs were carried out in 5 ll reactions, containing 2 ll Qiagen multiplex PCR buffer mix (Qiagen Inc), 0.2 lm labelled forward (Applied Biosystems, Carlsbad, CA, USA) and 0.2 lm unlabelled reverse primer, 0.5 ll of 109 BSA (New England Biolabs, Ipswich, MA, USA) and 1.5 ll DNA template. PCR conditions for microsatellites were as follows: initial denaturation (94 °C for 15 min), 45 cycles of denaturation (94 °C for 30 s), annealing (Ta for 45 s) and extension (72 °C for 45 s), and a final extension (72 °C for 30 min). PCR conditions for species identification followed protocols and conditions outlined in Mondol et al. (2009) and Mukherjee et al. (2007). All PCR products were separated using capillary electrophoresis on an ABI 3730xl sequencer, using GeneScan -500 LIZ ® size standard (Applied Biosystems) and alleles were scored on GENEMAPPER-4.1 (Applied Biosystems).

We carried out all pre-PCR procedures in sterile conditions in a separate room using aerosol barrier tips to minimize cross-contamination. Negative controls were included in all extractions and PCR to detect the presence of any exogenous DNA or reagent contamination. To account for error rates such as false alleles (FA) and allelic dropouts (ADO), we followed a modified multi-tube approach of Taberlet et al. (1996) and repeated each PCR four times for microsatellite analysis and accepted an allele score only if it amplified at least three times.

div.head: Data analysis
div.p: Because faecal DNA samples are more prone to error, we used the methods outlined in Dutta et al. (2012) to assess the reliability of our markers. We used MICRO-CHECKER 2.2.3 (van Oosterhout et al., 2004) to detect loci containing errors due to scoring or stuttering and estimated FA, ADO and calculated the cumulative P ID (probability of identity) and P ID (sibs) value (Waits et al., 2001) using GIMLET (Vali ere, 2002). Cumulative P ID values provide a measure of power of our panel of selected markers to distinguish individuals. Once we confirmed the reliability of our microsatellite scores, the variability of the microsatellite panel, and the power to distinguish between individuals, we used the program CONVERT (Glaubitz, 2004) for file conversions and enumeration of private alleles.

We measured genetic diversity using estimates of the number of alleles per locus (A), allelic richness (A R ), private allelic richness (P R ), observed (Ho) and expected (He) heterozygosity. We used CERVUS 2.0 (Marshall et al., 1998) to measure A, Ho and He and for individual identification. We used a stringent criterion of five out of seven matching loci to compare each multilocus genotype and identify unique individuals. We used HP-Rare (Kalinowski, 2004(Kalinowski, , 2005)), which uses a rarefaction method to compensate for unequal sample sizes, to compute A R and P R for each population.

We conducted tests for global and population-level deviations from Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium (HWE) and linkage disequilibrium (LD) using GENEPOP 4.0.10 (Rousset, 2008) with a Bonferroni correction (Rice, 1989) applied for multiple comparisons. We used ARLEQUIN with 10,000 permutations to test the statistical significance of pairwise F ST values (Weir & Cockerham, 1984) as a measure of genetic differentiation among the four TRs.

We measured D EST (Jost, 2008), an improved measure of genetic distance, using the web-based program SMOGD (Crawford, 2010). Gaggiotti et al. (1999) suggested that F ST is well suited when sample size and number of loci are relatively low, whereas D EST appears to be a more accurate and unbiased estimator of differentiation, and outperforms F ST for highly polymorphic markers like microsatellites and when sample sizes are large. We used 1000 bootstrap replicates, and the overall value for each population was calculated as the harmonic mean of D EST across loci, as executed by the software. In addition, we examined whether inter-population genetic differences could be explained by isolation by distance by conducting Mantel tests in ISOLDE (Rousset, 2008) within GENEPOP 4.0. We performed this test for both F ST and D EST . As the straight line Euclidian distance between TRs is not a true representation of their connectivity, we used a modified measure of geographic distance to better represent connectivity through forest cover. We measured the geographic distance between the TRs as the distance through forest cover on GOOGLE EARTH (Ver.6.0.3.2197, Mountain View, CA, USA).

As distance-based measures of population differentiation better reflect evolutionary and historic averages rather than current migration rates, we used individual-based Bayesian approaches to address contemporary genetic processes. We used two individual-based Bayesian clustering methods, STRUCTURE 2.3.3 (Pritchard et al., 2000) and TESS 2.3 (Chen et al., 2007). STRUCTURE is a non-spatial Bayesian clustering analysis that uses a Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) procedure to estimate the posterior probability that the data fit the hypothesis of K clusters [(Pr (X|K)]. We allowed the value of K to vary between 1 and 10 and performed 10 independent runs for each value of K. We used the admixture model with correlated allele frequencies (Falush et al., 2003) Diversity and Distributions, 19, 760-771, ª 2012 John Wiley & Sons Ltd without any additional population information using a burnin of 100,000 MCMC steps followed by an additional 100,000 iterations. The mean and standard deviation of Pr (X|K) from the 10 replicate runs were used to find the most likely value of K. We also used the ΔK method of Evanno et al. (2005) based on the second-order rate of change in log Pr (X|K) as implemented by the program STRUCTURE HAR- VESTER (Earl & von Holdt, 2011).

TESS (Chen et al., 2007) is a spatially explicit clustering program that builds individual neighbourhood networks using the Voronoi tessellation. In addition to multilocus genotypic data from individuals, TESS uses spatial information to define population structure without using predefined population information. We ran the TESS analysis for 10,000 burn-ins followed by 50,000 run-in sweeps for K (2-10) with 10 independent runs of each K. We used admixture models with the Dirichlet model of allelic frequencies and the interaction parameter (w) at the default value of 0.6, as suggested by the authors (Chen et al., 2007). We used the Deviance Information Criterion (DIC) and standard deviation to estimate the number of genetic clusters and to compare the performance of various models used in the analysis (Durand et al., 2009). To account for difference between runs and label switching, wherein replicate runs may switch labels for individual runs, we used the large K greedy algorithm in CLUMPP 1.1 (Jakobsson & Rosenberg, 2007) to align the 10 runs with the selected K.

To examine whether individuals originated from the TR in which their scats were collected, we used GENECLASS2 (Piry et al., 2004) with the assignment/exclusion of individuals option. We used a Bayesian approach (Rannala & Mountain, 1997) in combination with the resampling method of Paetkau et al. (2004), wherein we simulated 10,000 individuals at an alpha of 0.01. We also performed a second set of analyses with STRUCTURE, incorporating geographical sampling as prior population information (LOCPRIOR model) with all other parameters being identical to the other STRUCTURE analysis. We used a threshold of q ! 0.8 to assign individuals as residents of that subpopulation and those with q between 0.2 and 0.8 as individuals of admixed ancestry.

We selected the 'detect migrants' function in GENECLASS 2.0 because it is explicitly designed to identify first-generation migrants (Paetkau et al., 2004;Piry et al., 2004), that is, individuals born in a population other than the one in which they were sampled. We computed a likelihood ratio test to compare the population where the individual was sampled over the highest likelihood value among all available populations (L = L_home/L_max), while all other criteria were the same as above. We also used the 'detect migrants' function in STRUCTURE to identify migrants.

div.head: Genetic variability and summary statistics
div.p: We collected a total of 1411 felid scat samples, from which we identified 463 tiger and 287 leopard scats. The break-up of these 287 leopard positive samples from each sampling area was as follows: Melghat (42), Satpura (101), Pench (44), Kanha (95) and Corridor (5). We optimized a set of seven highly polymorphic loci to identify 217 individual leopards (geographic location of each individual is shown in Fig. S1) with a cumulative P ID of 1.44EÀ10 and P ID (sibs) of 5.24EÀ04. These microsatellites have been previously validated on blood and/ or tissue samples and have been found to perform well on faecal samples (Uphyrkina et al., 2001;Mondol et al., 2009). Details of microsatellite characteristics, success and error rates, and individual identification were previously described in Dutta et al. (2012) and are provided in Table S1. Eighteen individuals were recaptured twice, three individuals three times, two individuals four times and one individual seven times.

When samples from all reserves were pooled, six of the seven loci showed significant deviation from HWE. When reserves were tested separately, zero-four loci were in disequilibrium (Table 1), and no locus was consistently out of HWE. Six pairs of loci of 84 pairwise comparisons (four pairs in Pench and two in Satpura) were in significant LD after Bonferroni corrections, and these pairs were not consistent across the populations.

All loci were polymorphic in all populations, and genotypic data revealed high levels of genetic diversity at the seven microsatellite loci across TRs. In the global sample, the mean number of alleles was 13.29 with a range from 10 (FCA008) to 18 alleles (FCA304) and the mean observed (Ho) and expected (He) heterozygosity was 0.74 and 0.84, respectively. All individual reserves had high and comparable levels of polymorphism (number of alleles in all loci > 7) and average allelic richness (8.4-9.9, Table 1). The frequency of private alleles was highest in Satpura, followed by Melghat (Table S2).

Overall average F ST value for this landscape was 0.041 (SD 0.009). All pairwise comparisons of genetic differentiation using F ST and D EST were significant at P < 0.05 (Table 2). F ST and D EST values were highest between Kanha and Satpura. Mantel tests as implemented in ISOLDE in program GENE- POP suggested no significant correlation between geographic and genetic distance measures: F ST (r = 0.5, P = 0.67) or D EST (r = 0.6, P = 0.5).

div.head: Population structure
div.p: In the STRUCTURE analysis, the probability of the data, Pr (X| K), was highest for K = 5 (Fig. S2), beyond which the standard deviation of Pr (X|K) began to increase substantially. The ΔK approach, on the other hand, indicated the presence of two distinct genetic clusters with a smaller peak at K = 4 (Fig. S2a). In cases where the STRUCTURE program finds clustering solutions with similar probabilities at different values of K, the lowest value is typically the most accurate (Pritchard et al., 2000;Pritchard & Wen, 2004). Thus, although there is evidence for population subdivision at both K = 2 and K = 4, we consider K = 2 to be the optimal value in our study. At K = 2, Satpura TR forms one genetic cluster and the three other TRs form another cluster (Fig. 1). K = 4 shows a more fine-scale population structure, wherein each genetic cluster corresponds to each sampled TR.

In TESS, the DIC method infers a K of 4-5 (Fig. S2 (b)). However, in all runs where K > 2, the results were inconsistent between runs and individuals assigned to populations lacked any spatial coherency. At K = 2, all 10 independent runs produced consistent patterns and made geographic sense, wherein Satpura forms one cluster and the other three reserves form another genetic cluster (Fig. 1) and corresponds to the results from STRUCTURE. At K = 3 and K = 4, individual runs were inconsistent. At K = 3 (results not shown), seven of the 10 runs produced results similar to K = 2 (one cluster comprising Satpura, and the other cluster composed of the other TRs), whereas the third cluster contained only 4-7 individuals. At K = 4, three different kind of clustering patterns were observed in TESS, making its interpretation difficult (Fig. S3). Thus, we selected K = 2 as the most parsimonious answer.

We observed that in all of the runs at all values of K using both the programs, Satpura always clustered independently of the other populations. To test whether Satpura was driving the substructuring patterns observed, we ran STRUC- TURE excluding Satpura, using all the same parameters. In this analysis, STRUCTURE detected three genetic clusters that were highly admixed but corresponded to the three reserves (Fig. S4).

The rate at which individuals correctly assign to their sampled locality can be used as an assessment of population genetic structure (Manel et al., 2005). Using the GENECLASS assignment/exclusion test, 164 of the 217 individual leopards (75%) were assigned with the highest probability to the location from which they had been sampled. Many of the individuals that were 'misassigned' were subsequently identified as being of admixed ancestry and/or first-generation migrants. When we used the location prior model in STRUC- TURE, 84% (183 ⁄ 217) of the individuals had high probability of being residents (q > 0.8).

div.head: Identification of migrants
div.p: We identified nine migrants in this landscape. STRUCTURE and GENECLASS produced similar results and identified several of the same individuals (Table 3). STRUCTURE detected six migrants and GENECLASS detected eight migrants when the two genetic clusters were used as prior population information.

We also ran the analysis with the four TRs and used this analysis to identify which reserve was the source of the putative migrants. We found that six individuals were common to both outcomes, and all three migrants in Satpura TR were assigned to Melghat TR as their source population. STRUCTURE identified 26 individuals of admixed ancestry (Satpura-1, Melghat-13, Pench-7, and Kanha-5), which had q values between 0.2 and 0.8. These individuals could not be definitely identified as either migrants or residents.

div.head: Genetic variability in leopards
div.p: Leopards in central India showed high levels of genetic diversity. The observed and expected heterozygosity (0.74 and 0.84, respectively) were higher than those reported in the only other published study on Indian leopards (Mondol et al., 2009; Ho = 0.57, He = 0.68). All the TRs had similar values of Ho, He, A R and mean number of alleles, but the private allele richness for Satpura and Melghat was higher than for Kanha and Pench. Melghat and Satpura had five private alleles each, while Satpura had the highest frequency of private alleles (Table S2). Among the other subspecies, P. p. pardus has been reported to have the highest observed heterozygosity values of 0.803 (Uphyrkina et al., 2001) and 0.77 (Spong et al., 2000). Heterozygosity was slightly lower in P. p. fusca (0.696) and in P. p. saxicolor (0.616), much lower in P. p. kotiya (0.485) and P. p. japonensis (0.478) and lowest in P. p. orientalis (0.356) (Uphyrkina et al., 2001). P. p. nimr was genetically impoverished (Perez et al., 2006).

div.head: Population structure of leopards
div.p: The significant deviation from HWE for the global test indicated population substructuring, which was further confirmed by the low, but significant F ST values across all comparisons. When comparing pairwise differentiation measures (F ST and D EST ), it is important to note that the highest levels of differentiation observed are between Kanha and Satpura, populations that are not connected by corridors (Fig. 1); and the lowest values are between Kanha and Pench, populations that are connected by a corridor. The appropriate choice of the number of subpopulations, K, was not straightforward for this dataset as we found indications of K = 2 and K = 4. We selected K = 2 as the most parsimonious choice for our dataset based on higher q values, greater geographical concordance, support from spatial and non-spatial approaches, and recommendation from previous studies to choose the smallest value of K that captures the most structure in the data (Pritchard et al., 2000;Pritchard & Wen, 2004). Both STRUCTURE and TESS consistently identified one cluster that consisted of individuals almost exclusively from Satpura, whereas the other cluster consisted of individuals from the other three reserves. However, there is also evidence of ongoing differentiation, based on the second peak for second-order rate of change at K = 4, combined with the high frequency of accurate assignments. The further subdivision of the larger genetic cluster (Kanha-Pench-Melghat) into populations corresponding to geographic locations (Fig. S4) suggests that genetic subdivision is ongoing among leopards in this landscape. Leopards in the entire landscape are admixed, but the Satpura population is genetically more distinct from the other three reserves. Because Satpura is closest to the Narmada River, it could be genetically connected to protected areas across the river that are known to have good leopard populations (Jhala et al., 2011). Leopards could use the several riverine tributaries to move across the river (Athreya, 2006). Alternatively, there could be something specific to the corridor between Melghat and Satpura that prevents higher levels of gene flow. A fine-scale GIS analysis comparing factors such as forest cover, prey availability, road density, human population, land-use patterns and disturbances such as mines and dams is needed to determine which factors are responsible for the patterns that we observe. Although corridors in this landscape have several open-cast coal mines that have existed since as early as 1904 (Gee, 1940) and continue to exist all along the corridor (Singh & Shukla, 2004), we cannot conclusively determine how the Melghat-Satpura corridor differs from the other corridor in this landscape based on our study. The relationship between geographic and genetic distances (F ST and D EST ) among populations was not significant, suggesting absence of isolation by distance in leopard meta-population in our study area and that the observed subdivision cannot be explained by geographic distance between the TRs. Our analysis confirms that the results are not an artefact of sampling scale, nor are they driven by one population. Considering that leopards are habitat generalists (Bailey, 1993) and can disperse over long distances, these results are rather surprising and indicate the role of habitat fragmentation in increasing genetic isolation.

Leopards and predator-occupied forests were abundant in the 19th century in central India, when rewards were given for killing predators (Rangarajan, 1998). Conversion of forest lands into agricultural areas and demand for wood to construct railroads in India escalated the denudation of these Central Highland forests in the 19-20th century, leading to the degree of habitat fragmentation that we observe today (Rangarajan, 1998). Although leopards are often found in disturbed and degraded forests habitats, in close proximity to human habitation, and can survive on small prey like domestic dogs, cats, sheep and goats (Seidensticker et al., 1990;Edgaonkar & Chellam, 2002), given ample medium to large prey and some cover, leopards prefer undisturbed areas distant from human settlements (Ngoprasert et al., 2007;Gavashelishvili & Lukarevskiy, 2008). Leopards tend to avoid areas where tigers live at high densities because tigers are known to kill and out-compete leopards (Schaller, 1967(Schaller, , 1972;;Seidensticker, 1976;McDougal, 1988;Odden et al., 2010); and opportunistically steal their prey (Seidensticker, 1976). For example, in Sariska TR in western India, leopard densities have substantially increased since tigers were extirpated in 2004 (Chauhan et al., 2005;Mondal et al., 2012). Because tigers avoid human-dominated areas, these areas create a potential competition-free refuge for leopards (Odden et al., 2010). However, ecological escape from competition with other carnivores may lead to leopards coming into direct conflict with humans (Athreya, 2006).

Previous studies show that many other large carnivore species can be genetically differentiated at different levels due to habitat fragmentation. In a concurrent study in this same landscape, Sharma et al. (2012) reported low genetic substructuring of tigers, with lower F ST values, indicating higher gene flow than in leopards. In Tanzania (Spong et al., 2000), leopards had high gene flow and very low genetic differentiation. Pumas in Wyoming (Anderson et al., 2004) and Brazil (Miotto et al., 2011) did not have significant population substructuring, whereas Ernest et al. (2003) found significant genetic structure in California where urbanization has severely reduced and isolated natural habitats for the species. Jaguars were found to have high genetic structure and very low migration rates in the Upper Parana Atlantic forest due to severe habitat fragmentation over the past 30 years (Haag et al., 2010). Ultimately, even in highly vagile species, it appears that genetic differentiation varies by the landscape configuration, intensity of the habitat change and species life-history traits, ecology and behaviour.

Dispersal in the Central Indian leopard metapopulation Wright (1931) and Franklin (1980) projected that one successful migrant per generation would be sufficient to prevent population differentiation caused by genetic drift. More recent work suggests that 1-10 migrants per generation may be necessary (Mills & Allendorf, 1996) or even more than 10 migrants per generation (Vucetich & Waite, 2000). Our assignment tests allowed us to identify at least nine-first-generation migrants in our landscape. We identified three migrants in Satpura, one in Melghat, four in Pench and one in Kanha. Because six of the individuals identified with the four TRs as reference in the analysis were the same as those identified with two genetic clusters, we use the results from the former analysis to assign these migrant individuals to source TRs. Four of these six individuals were assigned to TRs connected by corridors. All three migrants in Satpura were assigned to Melghat, and one migrant in Pench was assigned to Satpura TR. These are pairs of TRs that have interconnecting corridors. Two individuals in Pench had the highest probability of having originated from Melghat, and one migrant in Kanha was assigned with highest probability to Satpura. Eleven per cent of all sampled individuals had admixed ancestry. The presence of a substantial number of admixed individuals in these areas suggests that leopards have been able to move across the landscape and reproduce, at least in the recent past.

div.head: CONCLUSION
div.p: This is the first study to assess the fine-scale spatial genetic structure of leopard populations at a landscape scale. Our results demonstrate that leopards in this landscape have high genetic diversity, and low genetic differentiation. We found two genetic subpopulations with indications of ongoing subdivision into four populations. This genetic substructuring cannot be explained by isolation by distance. Our study shows that migrants were assigned to populations that have corridors between them. These results provide evidence of the functionality of these corridors. Our study highlights that leopards, an adaptable and vagile species, can become genetically differentiated with increased habitat fragmentation.

Several coal mines have been proposed in the forest corridor between Satpura and Pench tiger reserves, and the widening of National Highway-7 project, which cuts through the Kanha-Pench corridor, is currently being debated in the Supreme Court of India. Increasing deforestation, agricultural intensification and urbanization are other factors that threaten these corridors. Our study conclusively demonstrates that these corridors are vital to maintaining genetic exchange, and we suggest corridors should be taken into consideration while preparing conservation management plans for this landscape.
